# The Lamp and the Wick

A lamp gives light only while three things hold together: the vessel, the oil, and the wick. The teacher in this chapter begins with that single image and refuses to leave it until the student has seen each part for what it is. The vessel is the body of discipline, the daily habits that keep a person steady. The oil is knowledge, gathered slowly, pressed out of long study the way oil is pressed from olives. The wick is the will, the small braided thing that actually touches the flame and is consumed by it.

The student objects at once. If the wick is consumed, then the cost of light is the destruction of the very part of the person that carries it. Why praise a lamp that eats itself? The teacher does not soften the point. Light is paid for. Every hour of clarity costs an hour of the self that produced it, and the person who refuses the cost keeps the wick intact and sits in the dark. The question is not whether the wick burns but whether it burns toward something or merely smolders.

From here the chapter turns to the oil. Knowledge that is never lit, the teacher says, turns rancid. It does not stay neutral in the jar. A person who gathers learning for its own sake, year after year, without letting any of it become conduct, will find that the store has soured — that the very arguments once gathered for the sake of truth now serve vanity, and serve it fluently. The student presses again: surely stored knowledge is at least harmless, a reserve against future need. The teacher answers with the second image of the chapter, the cistern and the spring. A cistern holds what was poured into it and goes stale; a spring gives constantly and stays sweet. The difference is not capacity but motion.

The third movement of the chapter binds the two images together. The vessel without oil is an ornament. Oil without a wick is a stored danger. A wick without a vessel gutters in the first wind. The teacher walks each pairing in turn, and under each pairing sits a kind of person the student is asked to recognize: the disciplined man with nothing to give, the learned man who gives nothing, the willing man with no frame to hold him steady. None of the three is wicked. Each is incomplete, and the incompleteness has a remedy that the other two parts supply.

The chapter closes with the question of who lights the lamp. The student assumes the answer is the teacher, and the teacher refuses the compliment. A hand lights a lamp, but the hand is not the fire. The teacher can trim the wick, fill the vessel, and shelter the flame from wind, and that is the whole of the office. What actually catches — the moment when knowledge, discipline, and will take light together — is not in the teacher's gift. The student asks what is left to do, then, beyond waiting. Keep the oil pressed, the teacher says. Keep the wick trimmed. The flame finds the lamp that is ready for it, and it finds no other.
